title: The Tianzhao Mandate
subtitle: The Mandate of Heaven and the empire of records
summary: A Mandate that can be lost, ministries for floods and for river spirits alike, a Registry of gods, the Closed Centuries, tea as leverage, and a classification problem called the Gates.
content:
> *"Heaven does not hurry. Neither do we."*
> — Tianzhao saying

The **Tianzhao Mandate** is an ancient bureaucratic empire whose whole way of life rests on one assumption: that reality has structure. Its people value harmony, composure, patience, hierarchy, long-term consequence, classification, continuity and the practical management of the spirits and powers it believes in.

Foreigners often call Tianzhao "mystical". That misses the point. What makes the Mandate unusual is not mysticism but integration. Government, ritual, engineering, spirits, law, medicine and ancestry are treated as parts of one larger ordered reality, to be understood, recorded and, where possible, administered. A Tianzhao official faced with a strange problem does not ask whether it is natural or supernatural. They ask which office is responsible for it.

None of this is magic, and educated Tianzhao officials are careful not to call it that. No talisman, rite or registered spirit has ever produced an effect a foreign scholar could measure. Before the Gates, the world had no magic at all; Tianzhao simply had the most thorough administration for the possibility.

*Heaven does not hurry* is not a recommendation to do nothing. It means that timing, position, relationship and consequence matter, and that the right action at the wrong moment is the wrong action.

This entry covers the Mandate's history and government. Its religious life is described in [[ten-thousand-offices-of-heaven|The Ten Thousand Offices of Heaven]], and how it looks and builds in [[under-heaven-under-ink|Under Heaven, Under Ink]].

## The Mandate of Heaven

The ruler of Tianzhao governs through the **Mandate of Heaven**, and may be styled the **Bearer of the Mandate** or the occupant of the **Celestial Throne**.

The Mandate is not guaranteed by blood. It depends on keeping proper relationship among the people, the state, the land, the ancestors, the institutions and the greater order of the cosmos. A dynasty can hold the Mandate legitimately and later lose it.

Tianzhao history is therefore understood in **dynastic cycles**. A dynasty rises and restores order. It builds institutions. Over time it becomes rigid or corrupt, loses harmony, and is replaced. The cycle is treated as both a historical pattern and a moral warning, and every official learns it. The Archive does not hold a full record of the dynasties themselves.

> **A senior official to a junior colleague, during a provincial unrest**
>
> "You are afraid the rebels will take the Mandate."
>
> "Aren't you?"
>
> "Rebels do not take the Mandate. Rebels are what you see when it has already been lost." The old official turned a page of the provincial grain report. "A dynasty does not lose Heaven because men with banners say so. It loses Heaven when the conditions that make men pick up banners have become impossible to deny. Look here, not at the banners. The granaries in this prefecture have been short for four years, and nobody wrote it down."
>
> He closed the report.
>
> "Write it down. Then we will see whether there is still a rebellion to worry about."

## An Empire of Records

Tianzhao is governed through an enormous bureaucracy of ministries, records, examinations, provincial administrations, legal offices, ritual officials and specialists. That bureaucracy is not merely a convenience. It reflects a conviction that runs through the whole culture: *if relationships can be understood, they can be administered*.

The civil service is closely tied to **examinations**, in fields that may include law, literature, history, mathematics, administration, ritual, astronomy, diplomacy and metaphysical theory. Scholarship is one of the great roads into government, examinations give officials their legitimacy, and the bureaucracy carries real cultural prestige. How exactly the examinations are structured, and who may sit them, are details the Archive has not yet recorded.

## The Celestial Ministries

Some of Tianzhao's ministries would be familiar anywhere: **Grain**, **Waters**, **Roads and Works**, **Foreign Courts**, **War**. Others puzzle foreign governments:

- **Heavenly Observation** concerns astronomy, unusual celestial phenomena, calendars, omens and long-term observation, and has taken an interest in certain measurements made since the Gates opened.
- **Ritual & Anomalous Affairs** deals with reported spirits, hauntings and supernatural disturbances, ritual law, anomalous events and the divine or spiritual beings the state recognises. It is not a secret police. It is closer to a ministry responsible for questions other states would split between religion, folklore, paranormal investigation, public safety and metaphysics. Its importance has grown enormously since the Gates appeared.

The reason both exist is that Tianzhao does not draw a sharp line between ordinary and supernatural administration. A flood may be at once a matter of engineering, agriculture, provincial law, ritual and a river spirit. Tianzhao's instinct is not to decide which explanation is "real". It is to work out which offices are responsible.

> **At a provincial office of Waters**
>
> "The embankment at the third bend has failed again," said the engineer, "and my repair order has been sitting on your desk for eleven days."
>
> The clerk drew the file toward him and uncapped his brush. "Before it can be routed, I must classify the failure. Is the problem engineering, agricultural, legal or divine?"
>
> The engineer thought about the silt, the farmers who had moved the drainage channels, the boundary dispute between two villages, and the shrine at the bend that nobody had tended since the old keeper died.
>
> "Yes," he said.
>
> The clerk sighed, and reached for four more forms.

## The Registry of Recognized Powers

Tianzhao may officially recognise supernatural beings. The state keeps a **Registry of Recognized Powers**, which can include city gods, river spirits, mountain spirits, local protectors and other old powers. Recognition may bring a title, a rank, a jurisdiction, a sanctioned temple and duties the being is expected to perform.

The principle behind the Registry is simple: supernatural power does not automatically stand outside government. If a being affects public order, Tianzhao may try to bring it into an administrative relationship. And a supernatural officeholder, like any other, can in principle be investigated, censured or demoted. As the joke goes in Tianzhao offices: *why should an officeholder be exempt from review merely because he is dead?*

How spirits are actually registered, reviewed or demoted is not set down here. See [[ten-thousand-offices-of-heaven|The Ten Thousand Offices of Heaven]].

## The Closed Centuries and the Quiet Court

For long periods Tianzhao deliberately restricted foreign access. These are remembered as the **Closed Centuries**. They were never complete isolation: trade continued, and foreign goods kept arriving. But Tianzhao preferred designated ports, controlled borders, formal diplomatic channels and firm limits on foreign political influence. Its own markets were already vast, and it did not believe it needed unrestricted foreign access to stay prosperous.

The same instinct shapes Tianzhao politics today. The Mandate prefers restraint, and its conflicts are often fought through delayed approvals, revoked permits, redirected invitations, changes in ceremonial precedence and privileges quietly allowed to expire. None of this is weakness. A Tianzhao official can destroy a diplomat's position without raising their voice, and frequently does.

## Tea

Tea has been grown in Tianzhao for centuries, and it is drunk across every social class in a great many forms. It is not merely a luxury or an export.

When Aurelia took up tea so enthusiastically that it became part of Aurelian national identity, Tianzhao found this amusing, useful, somewhat flattering and occasionally absurd. A senior Tianzhao diplomat is supposed to have summed up the official view:

> *"If they insist upon measuring civilisation in leaves, be grateful the leaves grow here."*

Tea is also leverage. Tariffs, access, plantations, shipping rights and favoured cultivars all give Tianzhao quiet influence over a great empire that cannot imagine life without its afternoon cup.

## Tianzhao and the Other Powers

- **The [Aurelian Empire](factions.html#aurelian-empire).** A sophisticated, polite rivalry. Aurelia wants open ports, treaties, access and influence; Tianzhao wants controlled engagement, formal protocol and limits on political intrusion. Neither side wants open war. Both prepare for it. Tea is one of many softer instruments on the table.
- **The [Kharad Compact](factions.html#kharad-compact).** An old trading partner. Tianzhao appreciates Kharadi patience, careful negotiation and long memory, and Kharadis are generally willing to accept Tianzhao's restrictions as long as the trade remains worthwhile.
- **The [Vardic Holds](factions.html#vardic-holds).** Tianzhao respects Vardic craftsmanship, metallurgy, engineering and precision, and finds the Vardic attitude to experiment useful, admirable and metaphysically reckless. *Tianzhao asks what a strange object is related to. A Vard asks what happens if it is heated.*
- **The [Vesper Republic](factions.html#vesper-republic).** Tianzhao admires Vesperian scholarship, science and intellectual energy, and is unimpressed by constant public agitation, political theatre and the assumption that visible argument is always productive. Older Tianzhao officials still occasionally call Vesper by its pre-revolutionary name, **the Kingdom of Solenne**. This may be bureaucratic habit, an extremely subtle insult, or both. Vesperians have a joke about it: that Tianzhao will formally recognise the Republic three centuries from now, and remark that it seems premature.

> **At a reception for the foreign delegations in Endros**
>
> "The Mandate thanks the delegation of Solenne for its kind gift," said the elderly Tianzhao envoy.
>
> "The Republic of Vesper," said the Vesperian representative, smiling.
>
> "Of course." The envoy inclined his head. Later in the evening: "Solenne's engineers have been most helpful at the Gates."
>
> "The *Republic's* engineers."
>
> "Naturally." And over the farewells: "Do convey our regards to the court of Solenne."
>
> The Vesperian representative smiled until the envoy had gone. Then she turned to her aide. "There is no court of Solenne. There hasn't been a court of Solenne for my entire life. He knows that."
>
> Her aide, who had been posted in Tianzhao for six years, said nothing at all.

## Industry Without Contradiction

Tianzhao does not assume that modern industry and old spiritual practice are opposed. Factories may hold shrines, ritual notices and protective inscriptions. Railways have developed their own local rites, spirit traditions and superstitions. Geomancers and engineers work side by side. Within Tianzhao, both are simply methods for managing different aspects of the same world. See [[under-heaven-under-ink|Under Heaven, Under Ink]].

## The Gates

Tianzhao's first explanation of the Gates was the obvious one within its worldview: **they might lead into the Spirit Realm**. The Mandate already had deep traditions concerning spirits, altered realms, dreams, death and supernatural geography, and the theory was taken very seriously.

The difficulty is that the evidence, as Tianzhao scholars report it, does not fit cleanly. Spirit specialists report that some spirits seem able to perceive Gates or interact with Gate phenomena, while others refuse to approach them or cannot perceive what lies beyond. Foreign observers point out that only the specialists can tell, and the specialists do not always agree. Some Gate worlds appear to have supernatural inhabitants of their own, and perhaps their own dead. None of this has settled into an agreed picture, and the result is a profound problem of classification.

Four broad theories now compete in Tianzhao: that Gate worlds are **Distant Provinces** of the same cosmic order; that they are **Outer Spirit Realms**; that they are **Foreign Heavens** with their own supernatural order; and, most uncomfortably, that some may be **Heavenless Places** outside Heaven's order altogether. They are described in [[ten-thousand-offices-of-heaven|The Ten Thousand Offices of Heaven]]. None is settled doctrine.

> **Minutes of a classification committee, Ritual & Anomalous Affairs (excerpt)**
>
> *Item four. An object recently recovered from beyond a Gate.*
>
> *The representative of Heavenly Observation proposed classification as a celestial phenomenon. Objected: it is not in the sky.*
>
> *The representative of Ritual proposed classification as a spirit-bearing object. Objected: no spirit has been observed, and two specialists have declined to stay in the room with it.*
>
> *The representative of Works proposed classification as equipment. Objected: nobody knows what it is for.*
>
> *After four hours, it was resolved that the object be entered provisionally under "Matters Awaiting Classification", and that a sub-committee be formed to determine whether such a category is permitted to exist.*

### The Pavilion of Celestial Affairs

Tianzhao maintains a significant presence in Endros, the **Pavilion of Celestial Affairs**. It is at once embassy, research institution, temple, observatory and archive: quiet, carefully ordered, gardened and closely administered. Visitors are received with perfect courtesy, and rarely see more than they were meant to. Secure underground rooms are said to be used for artifacts, dangerous objects and spiritual containment.
